title: Lifecycle hooks and effect()
summary: Run code when a component starts and stops with ngOnInit and ngOnDestroy, and react to signal changes with effect().

quiz.q: Put these in the order Angular runs them for a new component.
quiz.explain: The constructor runs first, `ngOnInit` once the inputs are set, `ngAfterViewInit` after the view is built, and `ngOnDestroy` when the component is removed.

quiz.q: Why do you clear a timer in `ngOnDestroy`?
options: Otherwise the timer keeps running after the component is gone
To make the page faster to load
quiz.explain: A timer started with setInterval lives on its own. If it is not stopped, it keeps running and wastes memory (a **leak**).

options: It runs again every time `count` changes
quiz.explain: An effect re-runs when any signal it reads changes. Use it for side effects such as logging, saving to localStorage or custom DOM work.

quiz.q: Fill in the interface name so the class promises an ngOnInit method.
quiz.explain: `implements OnInit` is optional but helps TypeScript check that you wrote `ngOnInit()` correctly.

exercise.task:
Finish `clock.component.ts`.

- The class `implements OnInit, OnDestroy`.
- In `ngOnInit()` start `setInterval(...)` that adds one to `seconds` (use `this.seconds.update(...)`) and store its result in `this.timerId`.
- In `ngOnDestroy()` call `clearInterval(this.timerId)`.
- In the constructor create an `effect(() => { ... })` that reads `this.seconds()` and logs it.
hints: Hooks are methods with fixed names. Start things in `ngOnInit` and stop them in `ngOnDestroy`.
`this.timerId = setInterval(() => this.seconds.update(s => s + 1), 1000);` An effect must be created in the constructor (or a field initialiser).

checks.name: The class implements OnInit and OnDestroy
checks.hint: Write class ClockComponent implements OnInit, OnDestroy.

The interval adds one to seconds
